$comment: Ruvyxa serves the same `public/` file from implementations that cannot share
code: the Rust static handler in crates/ruvyxa_dev_server/src/static_assets.rs
(`dev`, `start`, `preview`), and the JavaScript servers built from
handler). When they disagree the same byte-identical file is served with a
different Content-Type depending on where it is deployed.
They had disagreed. The Rust table knew nothing of .wasm, .woff, .woff2,
.gif, .ico, .map or .html and fell back to application/octet-stream, which
makes WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming refuse the module outright; the
JavaScript table knew nothing of .webmanifest and disagreed about the charset
on .json. Both tables were correct on their own and neither was checked
Add a case here first when changing what an extension serves as; a port that
drifts then fails in the language that drifted, not after deployment.
$contentTypeNotes: `html` is served as a document because a file placed in `public/` is authored
by the developer, not uploaded by a user; the JavaScript server already did
this and forcing a download in `ruvyxa start` only made the two disagree.
`txt` and `xml` carry an explicit charset to match the robots.txt and sitemap
declarations the build generates. `webmanifest` needs its own type or the
$fallbackNote: An extension with no entry, and a file with no extension at all, must be served as this rather than guessed at.
$caseNote: File systems preserve case, so `hero.PNG` reaches the handler spelled that way. Every implementation lowercases before lookup; these cases pin that.
$staticAssetNote: Extensions that only ever name a build or public asset. A request ending in
one of these has already missed both the client bundle directory and the
public directory, so a dynamic route must not render a page for it.
`txt` and `xml` are deliberately absent — a route may legitimately end in
either — even though both appear in `contentTypes` above, which answers a
different question: how to serve a file that does exist.
